question: What does reaching Moses's ashudd denote, and at what age?

positions.position: Completion or peak of physical strength and growth, without a fixed age.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Ṭabarī take the expression as vigor; al-Zajjāj says utmost bodily power; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say growth no longer increases. Biqāʿī includes all capacities. Al-Ālūsī prefers this general sense because timing varies by place, era and circumstance and a precise age needs a reliable report; he questions the inference from 46:15. Ibn Qutayba refers back to an earlier explanation. Abū Isḥāq allows the literal sense of attaining maturity.

positions.position: Thirty-three years.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid, Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās are repeatedly cited; al-Thaʿlabī's Ibn ʿAbbās report also says Adam's descendants were allotted sixty years and invokes 35:37. Sources commonly pair thirty-three for ashudd with forty for istiwāʾ; al-Kalbī is also reported for thirty-three.

positions.position: Puberty or adolescence, approximately fifteen years.
positions.reasons: Rabīʿa, Zayd ibn Aslam, Mālik and other exegetes identify the stage with puberty; al-Qurṭubī prefers it, citing the marriage-age test in 4:6. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports roughly fifteen, Muḥammad ibn Qays fifteen, and Iṣlāḥī calls it adolescence, requiring later poise.

positions.position: Eighteen years.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and Ibn Jubayr give eighteen; another group reports it, and a report from Imam al-Ṣādiq gives eighteen. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls eighteen the usual age.

positions.position: Twenty years.
positions.reasons: Al-Suddī, Mujāhid, Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and other reports give twenty.

positions.position: Forty years.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās and other exegetes identify full strength or full maturity itself with forty, though many other reports apply forty to istiwāʾ.

positions.position: Eighteen through thirty years.
positions.reasons: Al-Kalbī and Ibn ʿAbbās give a bodily-strength span; Ibn ʿAbbās describes a plateau from thirty to forty, then decline. Rāzī endorses the trajectory, observing that bodily power wanes while intellect increases. Bursawī gives the same span.

positions.position: Thirty to forty years.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj gives this range; some support it from 46:15, which couples full strength and forty, though al-Ālūsī says the inference is difficult. Al-Bayḍāwī associates this span with completed growth and maturing reason.

positions.position: Thirty-four years.
positions.reasons: Sufyān al-Thawrī supplies thirty-four; al-Qurṭubī presents it as the farthest limit of ashudd.

positions.position: Thirty years.
positions.reasons: Al-Suddī, an unnamed report and another group give thirty.

positions.position: Twenty-five years.
positions.reasons: ʿIkrima and another group give twenty-five.

positions.position: A few years after thirty, without an exact year.
positions.reasons: Attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Wāḥidī likewise says above thirty.

positions.position: Between thirty-three and thirty-nine.
positions.reasons: Reported by al-Zajjāj as one view.

positions.position: Eighteen through forty.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī attributes this range to Muqātil.

positions.position: Fifteen through forty.
positions.reasons: Reported by al-Jishumī as one interpretation.

positions.position: Eighteen through eighty.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī attributes this unusually broad span to al-Kalbī.

positions.position: Sixty-three years.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī attributes this to Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda while also saying istiwāʾ occurred at forty.

positions.position: Approximately seventeen through forty.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports this from al-Zajjāj.

positions.position: Thirty-six years.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes this to a large group.

positions.position: The point at which proof and moral responsibility are complete.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḥasan defines the stage by completion of obligation rather than a number.

positions.position: Visible maturity with complete physical and mental strength.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī reports signs of maturity and both faculties becoming complete.

turns_on: Whether ashudd marks puberty, peak bodily growth, a broad life span, or a fixed reported age; al-Ālūsī questions fixing an age without a reliable report.

question: What is the grammatical number and singular of ashudd?

positions.position: It is the plural of shidda.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh's analysis is reported by al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya; al-Jishumī and al-Nasafī compare niʿma/anʿum, while Abū al-Haytham adds the sense of strength and toughness. Al-Māwardī instead attributes shidda to al-Kisāʾī; al-Naḥḥās also lists the alternatives.

positions.position: It is the plural of shadd.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī are cited by Abū ʿUbayda, likening shadd/ashudd to baḥr/abḥur; al-Māwardī assigns this to Sībawayh. Rāzī says al-Farrāʾ treats shadd as analogical but unattested. Attributions vary across sources.

positions.position: It is plural in sense but has no singular of its own form.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿUbayda gives this analysis, also transmitted by al-Māwardī. Bursawī describes a singular form built on a plural pattern.

positions.position: It is a singular noun.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya record this alternative.

positions.position: Ashadd is not the only afʿal singular without tāʾ.
positions.reasons: Abū Isḥāq cites the lexicographers' aṣbaʿ; al-Naḥḥās calls denial of this comparison mistaken.

turns_on: Different analyses take the form as a plural of shidda or shadd, a plural without singular, or a singular noun; authorities' attributions differ.

question: What does Moses's istiwāʾ denote, and at what age?

positions.position: Mature, settled completion or balance of body and youth, without a fixed age.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and al-Zamakhsharī describe settled completion; al-Zamakhsharī cites al-Laqīṭ's poetry. Ibn Shajara emphasizes balanced bodily power; al-Bayḍāwī allows stature or intellect. Al-Ālūsī calls it explanatory of the preceding term. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says timing varies by person.

positions.position: Forty years.
positions.reasons: A large set of reports pairs forty with earlier bodily strength; Bursawī and al-Ālūsī cite 46:15, and al-Ālūsī mentions a poem and calls forty usual but not certain. The Study Quran relates forty to the traditional prophetic age and Muḥammad's first revelation.

positions.position: Completion of intellectual power, judgment, or temperamental poise.
positions.reasons: Rāzī prefers this distinction from bodily strength, explaining that intellect increases as physical power wanes. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ālūsī and Iṣlāḥī prefer mental completion; Iṣlāḥī says youth without poise is insufficient. Al-Junayd adds sound insight and readiness for divine address; the Study Quran reports adult sure footing.

positions.position: Bodily completeness, shape and stature.
positions.reasons: Rāzī records bodily-constitution readings; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares crops that thicken and stand upright in 48:29, distinguishing Moses's full tall build from Joseph's. A Prophetic description likens Moses to men of Shanūʾa, helping explain his fatal blow.

positions.position: Growth of Moses's beard.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qubayṣa/Abū Qubayṣa, Ibn Qutayba and an Imam al-Ṣādiq report make the sign of maturity the beard.

positions.position: The span from thirty to forty, followed by decline.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās report transmitted by al-Suyūṭī and al-Ālūsī.

positions.position: Sixty years.
positions.reasons: Makkī and Ibn Jarīr are separately reported for sixty; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the view weak.

positions.position: A settled adulthood between twenty-one and forty-two.
positions.reasons: Biqāʿī gives this interval after youth is complete.

positions.position: A stage from twenty-two to beyond forty.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī reports this further age range.

turns_on: Whether istiwāʾ completes bodily form, intellectual poise, or both, and whether reports fix it at forty or another age.

question: How do ashudd and istiwāʾ relate to each other?

positions.position: They are synonymous or the second reinforces the first.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports one view of balanced temperament and mature constitution; al-Ālūsī calls istiwāʾ explanatory; some commentators in the Study Quran agree. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects the synonymous reading.

positions.position: Ashudd is bodily strength; istiwāʾ is mature intellect and judgment.
positions.reasons: Rāzī favors this, as physical power wanes while intellect increases around forty; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ālūsī prefer it, the latter allowing age to vary by circumstance. Iṣlāḥī says youthful ability needs poise; the Study Quran places psychological maturity around forty.

positions.position: Ashudd is strength or adulthood; istiwāʾ is completed bodily form.
positions.reasons: Rāzī reports the strength/form and adulthood/perfection distinctions. Ibn ʿĀshūr holds that the latter term describes Moses's distinctive stature, comparing 48:29.

positions.position: They mark distinguishable stages, but the exact distinction is left open.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī says commentators distinguish them and directs the reader to his earlier discussions of Joseph and al-Anʿām.

turns_on: Whether the second term repeats the first or names a further completion, and whether that further completion is intellectual or physical.

question: What are the ḥukm and ʿilm given to Moses?

positions.position: Wisdom, sound understanding or reason, with religious knowledge before prophethood.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid says religious learning, reason and action before prophethood; Ibn Isḥāq specifies Moses's and his forefathers' religion, its laws and limits. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī and others give overlapping wisdom, jurisprudence and knowledge glosses. Rāzī prefers this against prophethood, citing wisdom paired with revelation at 33:34, prior upright character, and the reward clause. Al-Ālūsī prefers a prior gift because of narrative order and 28:13. Variants specify Abraham's law, God, or interests of both worlds. Al-Suddī specifically glosses ʿilm as understanding.

positions.position: Prophethood and its accompanying knowledge or religious science.
positions.reasons: Al-Suddī and Mujāhid are cited; Rāzī says the waw cannot itself date this relative to the killing. Al-Ālūsī reports a response that the gift summarizes the promised future mission after 28:13, while later verses detail it. Other versions specify religious law or both worlds.

positions.position: The bearing and conduct of wise, learned people before prophethood.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī say Moses did nothing foolish. Al-Bayḍāwī says this fits narrative order; al-Ālūsī explicitly prefers that fit over commissioning before the subsequent killing and migration.

positions.position: Knowledge is the Torah, and ḥukm is the prophets' Sunna.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī cites 33:34, the pairing of Scripture and wisdom in the Prophet's wives' houses; al-Ālūsī reports his view.

positions.position: Ḥukm is intellect or rational judgment.
positions.reasons: ʿIkrima says intellect; Asad calls it ability to distinguish right from wrong, Iṣlāḥī decision-making power, and the Study Quran reports judgment between people.

positions.position: Ḥukm is wisdom, and ʿilm is knowledge of God.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr gives this pairing; Asad speaks of deep spiritual consciousness; Iṣlāḥī adds that both capacities have levels and here precede prophetic wisdom.

positions.position: Ḥukm is understanding and intellect; ʿilm is prophethood.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid's report in al-Durr assigns prophethood specifically to ʿilm.

positions.position: Ḥukm is knowledge.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās gives this direct gloss.

positions.position: Ḥukm is strength.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī transmits Mujāhid's gloss.

positions.position: Ḥukm is the Quran.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim records this alternative from Mujāhid.

positions.position: The gift consists of the disciplines of sacred law.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī lists this separately among the alternatives.

positions.position: Ḥukm and ʿilm are theoretical and practical wisdom.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī gives this inward reading of the pair.

positions.position: God granted judgment and knowledge, with no narrower gloss.
positions.reasons: Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Kathīr affirm the gift without identifying a more specific referent.

positions.position: Prophetic wisdom before formal investiture, with knowledge of religious matters.
positions.reasons: The Study Quran transmits Ṭ's distinction between prophetic wisdom and formal investiture.

turns_on: Whether the gift is prophethood itself, preparatory wisdom and learning, or specific faculties or religious texts; opponents of prophethood invoke narrative sequence and the reward clause.

question: When did Moses receive this gift relative to his mission and the killing?

positions.position: Before prophethood, and before the killing of the Egyptian.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid, al-Zajjāj and other interpreters make it preparation; Rāzī explicitly places the gifts before the killing. Ibn ʿĀshūr says commissioning occurred only after Moses left Midian, citing 28:29. Al-Ālūsī traces the subsequent killing, migration and return, while Iṣlāḥī also puts prophetic wisdom later.

positions.position: The verse anticipates Moses's later prophetic commission after his migration and return.
positions.reasons: Al-Kāshifī places the commission after the Midian migration, on return to Egypt; al-Ālūsī reports supporters who take this verse as a summary of the promise in 28:13, later told in detail. Ibn ʿĀshūr points to 28:29.

positions.position: The conjunction does not determine whether prophethood preceded or followed the killing.
positions.reasons: Rāzī says the waw introducing the entry into the city lacks necessary sequence; al-Ālūsī's reported prophethood advocates likewise say waw need not order events.

positions.position: Moses attained the described spiritual maturity after the events beginning in verse 15.
positions.reasons: Asad cites Moses's statement at 26:20 as evidence.

turns_on: Whether the clause describes prior preparation or anticipates a later mission, and whether waw establishes chronology.

question: How did preprophetic learning affect Moses's standing among the Israelites?

positions.position: He knew ancestral religion and had followers among the Israelites.
positions.reasons: Ibn Isḥāq specifies the rules and limits of Moses's and his fathers' religion; al-Wāḥidī says Israelites listened and followed, while al-Qurṭubī gives the number nine before prophethood.

positions.position: He led Israelites before migration and knew useful ancestral teachings through inspiration or transmitted reports.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī says Israelites brought important affairs to him and obeyed his commands; knowledge could be inspired or inferred from prophetic ancestors' beliefs and laws or reliable reports. He considers this perhaps preferable to a Kashshāf report.

positions.position: Palace education accompanied God's gift, and Moses already saw Pharaoh's injustice.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu says Moses was educated in the palace and before his mission recognized Pharaoh's oppression of the Israelites.

turns_on: Whether the notes describe a following, active leadership and inspired knowledge, or palace education and moral awareness.

question: Must prophets be commissioned at forty?

positions.position: A report says every prophet was commissioned at forty.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī record the universal claim; Bursawī says most hold Muḥammad was commissioned at forty and some extend this to all prophets. The Study Quran calls forty the traditional age of prophethood and Muḥammad's first revelation.

positions.position: Forty is not a requirement for every prophet.
positions.reasons: Bursawī reports Jesus at thirty-three, Joseph at eighteen, and John at two or three; he also cites Sahl al-Tustarī's spiritual knowledge before puberty.

turns_on: Whether the report about forty is universal; the opposing note supplies younger prophetic examples.

question: Why is this stage fitting for Moses's divine gift or mission?

positions.position: Mature intellect, insight and character prepare him for divine address and prophethood.
positions.reasons: Al-Junayd says readiness follows sound insight and complete reason. Al-Qushayrī says God completes the preparation of eminent people and prophets. Rāzī calls prophethood the highest rank requiring knowledge and uprightness; al-Biqāʿī calls wisdom and knowledge anticipatory preparation.

positions.position: God's choice at this age signals exceptional, unacquired growth beyond ordinary human decline.
positions.reasons: Biqāʿī cites 36:68: ordinary people stop gaining faculties after youth, then decline; chosen prophets and righteous followers can still gain strength and knowledge without acquisition, making Moses's innate gift miraculous.

turns_on: The notes give preparation and miraculous divine choice as distinct explanations.

question: What does wisdom or knowledge require of its possessor?

positions.position: A truly wise and learned person acts on knowledge; failure to act is ignorance.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj cites 2:102; al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī and al-Nasafī repeat that acting is integral. Al-Biqāʿī defines wisdom as perfected action through knowledge, and says knowledge is supported by wisdom.

positions.position: The gifts include clear self-knowledge and awareness of new favors from God.
positions.reasons: Al-Junayd's inward gloss ties the gift to readiness for divine address.

turns_on: The notes describe practical action and inward self-knowledge as dimensions of the gift.

question: Who are the muḥsinīn in the reward clause?

positions.position: Those who believe in God or affirm His oneness.
positions.reasons: Muqātil says believers; al-Kalbī says people of monotheism.

positions.position: Moses, his mother, and by extension everyone who does good.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī cites her obedience and trust in placing Moses in the river and God's safe return of him; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Biqāʿī extend the pattern. The Study Quran reports the mother's reward as her son, his return, and his intelligence.

positions.position: People who use their abilities fully and well.
positions.reasons: Iṣlāḥī says wisdom rewards this use, whereas unused youth and abilities are wasted.

positions.position: People endowed with virtues who walk the path of justice.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī gives this inward characterization.

turns_on: Whether the clause identifies believers, the historical exemplars Moses and his mother, or a quality of virtuous conduct.

question: What is the recompense promised to doers of good, and how is it related to the gift?

positions.position: God grants wisdom and knowledge as reward for obedience and goodness, leading to Paradise.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī names Moses's obedience, patience and avoidance of prohibitions and extends reward to every obedient messenger and servant. Al-Zajjāj, Abū Isḥāq, al-Wāḥidī and al-Nasafī explain that knowledge and wisdom lead to Paradise. Ibn Isḥāq connects the gift with the reward formula; Iṣlāḥī links wisdom to using ability well.

positions.position: God repays Moses's mother, Moses, and other good-doers with deliverance and further gifts.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī lists his mother's trust, her child's safe return and Moses's later reason, wisdom and prophethood; al-Biqāʿī stresses their reliance on God alone. The Study Quran reports a son, his return and judgment; Bursawī says those who join their pious company receive the best recompense.

positions.position: Prophethood itself is not earned by deeds.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī says Moses's character qualified him for the mission, not that deeds earned it. Rāzī argues that calling prophethood recompense would imply every good-doer becomes a prophet; al-Ālūsī says it sits uneasily with the clause. The Study Quran transmits Rāzī's merit objection.

positions.position: On a prophethood reading, the clause may generalize reward, or reward higher degrees of prophetic nearness.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports defenders who count God's gifts to Moses and his mother as recompense by generalizing attribution; he allows increased nearness to God as recompense while denying that prophethood itself is earned. Prophets differ in nearness. He also notes that the every-benefactor objection need not defeat the reading.

positions.position: Divine favors arrive at their appointed time, so seekers should remain patient.
positions.reasons: Bursawī says delay should not cause despair and illustrates repayment of charity with a report of a beggar, a wolf taking a donor's child, her prayer, and the child's rescue unharmed.

turns_on: Whether the gift itself is recompense, and whether prophethood can be described as a reward for deeds.

question: What inward stages are described by Moses's maturity?

positions.position: Ashudd is spiritual youth and perfected primordial nature; istiwāʾ is perfection followed by detachment from the soul's attributes.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī maps both successive stages onto spiritual development.

positions.position: Istiwaʾ is balance of hope and fear, humility and dignity, dependence and autonomy.
positions.reasons: The Study Quran transmits Aj's inward account of the poise at which true wisdom starts.

turns_on: The inward readings identify different balances or stages.

question: How does this wording relate to Joseph's story and other Quranic parallels?

positions.position: It closely parallels Joseph 12:22 and the same recompense formula elsewhere.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī refer explanation to Joseph; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes Joseph lacks the added istawāʾ, which he relates to Moses's tall full build. Asad notes near identity. The Study Quran cites 6:84, 12:22, 37:80, 105, 110, 121, 131, 77:44, and its notes at 29:69 and 37:80.

positions.position: Joseph received revelation in youth, whereas Moses received it after forty, explaining why their maturity wording differs.
positions.reasons: Bursawī contrasts 12:22, which mentions only full strength, with this verse's added istiwāʾ.

positions.position: The maturity language also relates to legal independence of orphans.
positions.reasons: The Study Quran links 12:22, 6:152, 17:34 and the maturity-age discussion at 4:6.

turns_on: The notes explain the added wording through Moses's stature or the different age of revelation, while also noting broader parallels.

question: How does verse 14 fit the surrounding account of Moses?

positions.position: It is a chronological interlude after the promise to Moses's mother was fulfilled.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr says the promise in 28:7 was fulfilled by the return in 28:13, prompting this overview. Al-Ālūsī also tests readings against the narrative sequence; Asad instead places spiritual maturity after the events beginning at 28:15, citing 26:20.

positions.position: The telling of Moses and Pharaoh varies in wording, order and detail across retellings for distinct nuances.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhān surveys 28:3–43 and contrasts Joseph's collected narrative in one sūra with earlier scripture's separate single tellings.

positions.position: Moses grew up with Pharaoh and his wife after weaning, before the later killing and flight to Midian.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī reports his childhood household; the Study Quran summarizes the killing in 28:15–20 and flight in 28:21–22.

positions.position: The described maturity followed the events beginning at verse 15.
positions.reasons: Asad cites 26:20.

turns_on: Whether the maturity notice summarizes an earlier stage or later spiritual growth.

question: What circumstances and location are reported for Moses's entry into the city in the next verse?

positions.position: Moses came from Khanin, two farsakhs away, at midday.
positions.reasons: Muqātil names the village, distance and time.

positions.position: He concealed his opposition to Pharaoh and entered the city at night.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu surmises that his opposition spread among relatives, leading him to hide.

positions.position: The city was the Egyptian city where Pharaoh resided.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu attributes this to most commentators.

positions.position: The city was Aynişems, formerly an independent settlement.
positions.reasons: Attributed to al-Ḍaḥḥāk by Kur'an Yolu.

positions.position: The city was Cairo.
positions.reasons: Attributed to al-Shawkānī by Kur'an Yolu.

positions.position: The city was Memphis, northern Egypt's center.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu reports this identification from some.

turns_on: Reports differ on the city's identification and whether Moses entered at midday or at night.

question: What is said of the sūra's revelation setting?

positions.position: The whole of al-Qaṣaṣ is Meccan.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī transmits this from al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrima.

question: What ancillary Arabic poetic usage is recorded with the verse's discussion?

positions.position: In a line recited by al-ʿUqaylī, the first ʿām in 'year after year' is redundant.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ transmits the line as a linguistic example; the note does not connect its wording directly to any word of 28:14.
